# Reward Engine: Reward-Centric Self-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents

Litong Feng Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team Affiliation: Equal
contribution.    Ji Qi Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team Affiliation:
Equal contribution.    Yiran Cheng Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team
   Shaowu Pan Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team    Xinyu Zhang
Affiliation: Huawei openJiuwen Team    Qijun Li Affiliation: Huawei
openJiuwen Team

###### Abstract

Open-ended tool agents can complete the same objective through different
tool paths, and their quality depends jointly on the interaction trace,
environment state, and final artifacts, so such tasks rarely admit an
executable ground-truth reward. The central challenge is therefore to
construct a reward from existing experience that exposes the current
policy’s failures while remaining stationary during optimization. We
introduce Reward Engine, which, like a self-motivated student, first
works out what success requires and then optimizes toward it. From the
task and initial trajectories, it builds a RewardPack of testcases for
required correctness and rubrics for graded quality, each executed as a
check that returns a judgment with evidence. The frozen RewardPack then
guides the agent to revise and select its outputs, and can also serve as
a reward for reinforcement learning. On WorkBuddy Bench Office and
Claw-Eval, the constructed reward largely agrees with the benchmark
graders, not reversing their ordering on 82.3% and 80.5% of candidate
pairs. Used to revise executions, it raises three-run consistency
($`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$) over Baseline from 45.0% to 54.0% and from 78.4%
to 83.7%.

²²footnotetext: Ji Qi is also affiliated with the Department of

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.22915v1/motivation_analogy.png)

Figure 1: From a self-motivated student to a self-motivated agent. (a) A
student facing a new task identifies hard constraints and room to excel.
(b) Testcases (required correctness) and rubrics (graded quality), bound
to executable checks, form a frozen RewardPack. The
reinforcement-learning branch is a possible extension and is not
evaluated.

Tool agents are increasingly asked to do open-ended work, such as
reconciling spreadsheets, drafting reports from mixed-format files, or
triaging tickets \[[Yao et al., 2025](#bib.bib36); [Tencent Youtu Lab et
al., 2026](#bib.bib17); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)\]. Unlike
verifiable tasks such as math with final answers or code with unit tests
\[[Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib23); [Jimenez et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)\], whose rewards directly drive reinforcement learning
\[[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)\], these tasks come with no reward:
many solutions are acceptable, and quality depends on the trace,
environment state, and delivered artifacts. Constructing the reward thus
becomes the key, and harder, problem; without it, an agent can neither
critique and select among its attempts nor train on them. Common proxies
fall short: a weekly report whose completion rate reads 92% although the
source rows give 78% passes a file-existence check and can pass a
holistic model judge, whose verdicts depend on presentation and ordering
\[[Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)\].
Like a self-motivated student facing an untaught task, the agent must
first work out which constraints must hold and where there is room to
excel
([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")),
and the resulting reward must meet three requirements:

- •
  Evidence-grounded: each criterion, whether a hard constraint
  (testcase) or graded quality (rubric), must be judged by recomputing
  it from the artifact, trace, and environment and returned with a
  receipt, such as “expected 78%, observed 92%: fail”. The receipt tells
  a critic what to fix and a selector why one candidate ranks higher,
  and it keeps a violated requirement apart from an unreadable file or
  missing evidence.
- •
  Tested before use: a drafted check can itself be wrong, for instance
  by reading the wrong column or accepting a near miss, so the reward
  must be tested against labeled counterexamples before the agent relies
  on it, and a repair must not break cases it already judged correctly.
- •
  Stationary: the reward must stay fixed while the agent is revised or
  selected against it and change only between rounds; otherwise an
  apparent gain may come from a moved target rather than a better
  output.

![Refer to caption](2610.22915v1/reward_engine_overview.png)

Figure 2: Reward Engine in three stages. _1. Build reward (blue):_
criteria and executable checks are tested and repaired before a
RewardPack is frozen. _2. Execute by reward (orange):_ the frozen pack
supports revision and selection. _3. Update reward (green):_ products,
receipts, and use-time defects inform the next construction round.
Benchmark scores are reserved for evaluation.

Existing evaluators and reward-construction methods meet these
requirements only in part
([Table 5](#A1.T5 "In Appendix A Comparison with related methods ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Comparison with related methods ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
Model judges, rubric judges, and trained verifiers \[[Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7); [Kim et al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Saad-Falcon et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Gunjal et al., 2026](#bib.bib10); [Cobbe et al.,
2021](#bib.bib23)\] score outputs, but their judgments are not bound to
re-runnable procedures, and at most partially record the evidence behind
them \[[Zhuge et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Rao and Callison-Burch,
2026](#bib.bib11)\]. Reward-construction methods write executable reward
code or tests \[[Ma et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Xie et al.,
2024](#bib.bib30); [Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib31)\] but keep no
evidence receipts, so a violated requirement cannot be told apart from a
broken check. Most importantly, none tests the reward for a task on
labeled counterexamples before optimizing against it, or accepts a
repair only if earlier agreement is preserved; the closest, EvoRubrics
\[[Ding et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)\], adapts its rubrics adversarially
but updates them at every training step, so the target moves while it is
used. What is missing is a reward that is evidence-grounded, tested
against counterexamples before use, and held fixed while the agent is
optimized against it.

We introduce Reward Engine
([Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"))
to close this gap: it builds such a reward for each task and uses it to
improve the agent’s deliverable. Each round has three stages:

Build reward. From the task and a few initial trajectories, never hidden
answers or benchmark scores, a Jury drafts the task’s obligations as
testcases or graded rubrics, and a Builder binds each to an executable
check that returns a judgment with an evidence receipt
([Sections 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
and [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Constructing criteria and checks ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
A quality-control loop tests the reward on labeled control, error, and
boundary cases and accepts only repairs that lose no previously matched
case; the result is frozen as a _RewardPack_
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

Execute by reward. A Critic turns failed criteria into revision
feedback, and a Jury ranks the revision with the round’s other
candidates; a candidate replaces the fresh task-only one only if it
ranks strictly higher and fails no test the task-only candidate passes
([Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

Update reward. Products, receipts, and defects found during use inform
only the next RewardPack, so the reward never shifts while it is used; a
meta loop across task families, which we do not evaluate, can further
refine how rewards are built. On WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval,
the RewardPack does not reverse the benchmark grader’s ordering on 82.3%
and 80.5% of candidate pairs and raises $`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$ over
Baseline from 45.0% to 54.0% and from 78.4% to 83.7%
([Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

Our main contributions are (1) An evidence-grounded RewardPack of
testcases for required correctness and rubrics for graded quality, built
from the task and initial trajectories, each criterion and rubric bound
to an executable evidence check
([Sections 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
and [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Constructing criteria and checks ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
(2) Reward-centric self-improvement, in which the frozen RewardPack
guides Critic-driven revision and Jury selection of the deliverable and
is updated only between rounds
([Sections 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
and [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
(3) Two-benchmark evidence on WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval that
the RewardPack largely agrees with the benchmark graders and raises the
delivered output’s pass rate over Baseline
([Section 4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

## 2 Problem setup

##### Tasks and objective.

A task supplies public requirements $`x`$, including its input files,
and a tool environment. An actor $`\pi`$, a language model in a fixed
tool harness, takes actions $`a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t})`$ given its
context $`h_{t}`$ and delivers a _product_ $`y`$: the artifact, its
interaction trace, and the resulting environment state. The task’s
quality $`q(y)`$, here the benchmark grader’s score, is hidden. The
system sees only the public information $`\mathcal{I}`$: $`x`$, updates
from the task’s own (possibly simulated) user, public background
knowledge the task does not forbid, the execution history, and a few
initial runs $`\mathcal{B}`$ of $`\pi`$ on $`x`$ alone. From
$`\mathcal{I}`$ it must (i) construct a reward $`R`$ whose judgments
track $`q`$ and (ii) use $`R`$ to deliver a product $`y^{\star}`$ of
higher $`q`$ than $`\pi`$ attains alone;
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
measures (i) by order agreement with the grader and (ii) by the scores
and pass rates of $`y^{\star}`$. The weights of $`\pi`$ are never
updated: what evolves is the reward and the process that builds it.
Hidden answers and grading outputs are excluded by design.

##### Reward.

A reward binds criteria to checks, and running a check on a product
returns a judgment with its evidence:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
R=\{(c_{i},\kappa_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m},\qquad R(y)=\bigl(\kappa_{i}(y;x)\bigr)_{i=1}^{m},\qquad\kappa_{i}(y;x)=(z_{i},e_{i}).
``` |  | (1) |

A criterion $`c_{i}`$ is a *testcase* (required correctness,
$`z_{i}\in\{\mathsf{pass},\mathsf{fail}\}`$) or a *rubric* (graded
quality, $`z_{i}\in\{\mathsf{fail},\mathsf{partial},\mathsf{full}\}`$
against written anchors); $`z_{i}=\bot`$ means no judgment, and several
bound tests give a tuple
([Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
A check $`\kappa_{i}`$ is a stored, re-runnable procedure, either code,
such as recomputing a rate from source rows, or a model judgment over
evidence it first locates, so it need not be deterministic. The
*receipt* $`e_{i}`$ references the inspected evidence and records the
execution status, keeping apart an observed violation (a failing
judgment), insufficient evidence ($`\bot`$, normal status), and a check
that did not run ($`\bot`$, error status). A *RewardPack* stores one
version $`R_{v}`$ with the records needed to audit and re-run it
([Table 7](#A2.T7 "In B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

$`R(y)`$ is a vector, not a scalar, so each consumer states its use: the
Critic turns failing judgments and receipts into feedback
([Eq. 5](#S3.E5 "In Critic feedback. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"));
selection ranks candidates by a Jury that reads artifacts and receipts,
and rejects any candidate that fails a test the task-only candidate
passes
([Eq. 6](#S3.E6 "In Candidates and selection. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"));
and the grader comparison orders candidates by the share of resolved
criteria that pass. Reinforcement learning would need a similar
reduction and is not evaluated.

##### Requirements.

The requirements of
[Section 1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
become conditions on $`R`$. *Evidence-grounded*: every judgment other
than $`\bot`$ carries a receipt naming the parts of $`y`$ and $`x`$ it
used. *Tested before use*: $`R`$ is first run on labeled cases
$`(y_{j},i_{j},z^{\star}_{j})`$, each a product, a targeted criterion,
and a reference label assigned blind to $`R`$; $`R`$ *agrees* on a case
if $`z_{i_{j}}=z^{\star}_{j}`$, is *unresolved* if $`z_{i_{j}}=\bot`$,
and *disagrees* otherwise, and a repair must keep every case already
agreed on
([Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
*Stationary*: of the three layers, the actor $`\pi`$, the reward $`R`$,
and the construction state $`\phi`$ that builds rewards
([Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Constructing criteria and checks ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")),
only $`\pi`$ is fixed throughout. We index actor steps by $`t`$, rounds
by $`n`$, reward versions by $`v`$, and updates of $`\phi`$ by $`k`$.
Quality control may produce several versions within a round; the last is
frozen for the round’s execution stage, where feedback changes only the
context $`h_{t}`$, and revisions of $`R`$ or $`\phi`$ take effect only
at round boundaries. A gain within a round therefore comes from a better
product, not a moved target.

## 3 Reward Engine

[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Candidates and selection. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
gives the per-task procedure over the three stages of
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents");
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
gives the notation, RewardPack schema, and implementation details.

### 3.1 Constructing criteria and checks

##### Jury.

Three Jury members draft obligations from the public task before seeing
any artifact, then revisit them against the initial task-only runs
$`\mathcal{B}`$, which show where the current policy falls short and
where acceptable solutions differ. A reducer merges the drafts into
criteria, each marked as a testcase or a rubric, keeping each
criterion’s source, applicability, and fail/partial/full anchors;
unresolved obligations stay visible. For the weekly report, Jury fixes
the reporting period and the completion-rate definition. An obligation
that no member proposes remains an omission that this review cannot
detect
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Construction and regression-gated repair ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

##### Builder.

Builder turns each criterion into executable tests, refining its
fail/partial/full anchors into the rubric a model-judge check applies
(Reward Builder), and binds them to inputs, tools, and judgment
procedures (Harness Builder); for the weekly report, the completion-rate
test recomputes the rate from the source rows. Construction is guided by
the *construction state* $`\phi=(\omega,\mathcal{M})`$, which pairs
Strategy $`\omega`$ with Memory $`\mathcal{M}`$, under a scope, delivery
contract, and budget:

|     |                                      |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{0}\sim\Build_{\phi}(\mathcal{I}),
       ```                                   |     | (2) |

where $`\Build`$ may instead return an explicit construction failure.
Each receipt of
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In Reward. ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
is bound to the inspected artifact, environment snapshot, inputs, scope,
and check version, so a judgment can be audited, and a receipt is reused
only when its artifact, environment snapshot, scope, and check version
all still match
([Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

##### Strategy and Memory.

Strategy $`\omega`$ holds module guidance and settings for quality
control (QC,
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")),
and Memory $`\mathcal{M}`$ stores construction lessons with their
sources and validation status. Stage 3 of every round
([Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"))
adds lessons to Memory, so Memory grows within the inner loop, whereas
Strategy changes only in the meta loop of
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Candidates and selection. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
That loop proposes updates of $`\phi`$ on training task families and
selects them on disjoint validation families; it changes how evaluators
are built ($`\phi`$), not how tasks are solved ($`\pi`$). We do not
evaluate the meta loop:
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
runs the inner loop only.

### 3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair

A drafted check may be implemented incorrectly, or an obligation may be
missing or mis-stated. QC (Adversarial Testing and Repair & Validate in
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"))
targets both. At version $`v`$ it constructs labeled cases of the form
defined in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"),

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{v}=\{(y_{j},i_{j},z^{\star}_{j})\}_{j}\sim\Attack(R_{v},\mathcal{I}),
``` |  | (3) |

of three kinds: *control* cases should pass, *error* cases violate the
targeted criterion (e.g., an edited cell that breaks the completion
rate), and *boundary* cases are near misses. Reference judges, which are
language models, label anonymized cases against public evidence, blind
to the RewardPack, the attack rationale, and the predicted label. The
cases join the repair ledger $`Q_{v}=Q_{v-1}\cup A_{v}`$, with
$`Q_{-1}=\varnothing`$. Agreement, disagreement, and unresolved
judgments are as defined in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents");
judgments are recorded once per version and replayed. Let
$`G_{v}\subseteq Q_{v}`$ be the cases on which $`R_{v}`$ agrees and
$`F_{v}\subseteq A_{v}`$ the new cases on which it disagrees. A case
whose repair is rejected stays in the ledger as a disagreement and is
not targeted again, although a later accepted repair that also fixes it
adds it to the agreed cases.

Jury revises missing or mis-stated obligations and Builder repairs
checks, producing a *minimal* candidate
$`\widetilde{R}\sim\Repair_{\phi}(R_{v},F_{v})`$ that preserves
unrelated criteria and checks and remeasures only affected bindings.
Writing $`\widetilde{G}`$ and $`\widetilde{U}`$ for the cases of
$`Q_{v}`$ on which the candidate agrees and is unresolved, it is
accepted only if

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{no regression:}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle G_{v}\subseteq\widetilde{G},`$ |  | (4) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{fixes a failure:}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle F_{v}\cap\widetilde{G}\neq\varnothing,`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{no unresolved comparison:}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\widetilde{U}=\varnothing.`$ |  |  |

The implementation also requires unchanged known reference labels and
supported fresh boundary cases around the repair
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Construction and regression-gated repair ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
The last condition of
[Eq. 4](#S3.E4 "In 3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
is strict: a ledger case that stays unresolved under every version
blocks later repairs until its evidence is resolved, and QC then keeps
the incumbent. Then $`R_{v+1}=\widetilde{R}`$ if the candidate is
accepted and $`R_{v+1}=R_{v}`$ otherwise, and QC continues until an
attack finds no failure or its budget is exhausted.

The acceptance rule makes agreement monotone,
$`G_{v}\subseteq G_{v+1}`$: a reference case the reward once matched is
never lost
([Proposition 1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Ratchet). ‣ C.1 Ratchet property ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
in
[Section C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Ratchet property ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
The guarantee has three limits. It is relative to the reference labels,
which are themselves fallible model judgments whose accuracy we do not
measure, so a systematically wrong label is kept as firmly as a correct
one. It covers only accumulated cases; accuracy on unseen artifacts
requires held-out evaluation. And it covers only QC repairs: at a round
boundary (stage 3), BoundaryUpdate in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Candidates and selection. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
keeps, rebuilds, or revises the reward under the caller’s rules, which
need not preserve $`G_{v}`$
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Construction and regression-gated repair ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

### 3.3 Using a frozen reward

After QC the latest version is frozen for execution (stage 2 of
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"));
we write $`R`$ for it below. Products, receipts, and defects found
during use inform construction only at the next round boundary (stage
3).

##### Critic feedback.

Actor steps append actions and observations to the context, and the
terminal review of a reward-guided delivery $`y_{T}`$ appends Critic
feedback computed from targeted checks of the frozen reward:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{actor step:}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}),`$ |  | $`\displaystyle h_{t+1}=h_{t}\oplus(a_{t},o_{t+1}),`$ |  | (5) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{terminal review:}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle f\sim\Critic_{R}(\cdot\mid h_{T},R_{S}(y_{T})),`$ |  | $`\displaystyle h^{\prime}_{T}=h_{T}\oplus f,`$ |  |  |

where $`R_{S}(y_{T})`$ restricts
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In Reward. ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
to the set $`S`$ of checks the review targets (at most three in our
runs). Critic suggests, requests clarification, or abstains, citing
supporting receipts. When the review is nonempty and budget remains, the
same actor session continues from $`h^{\prime}_{T}`$, and the revised
delivery is then rechecked. This loop uses the limits and stopping
conditions in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Implementation details ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"),
with $`\pi`$ and $`R`$ fixed throughout. Because unselected checks stay
unverified, stopping does not certify that the whole RewardPack passes.

##### Candidates and selection.

Each round generates three candidates: a *task-only candidate*
$`y^{\circ}`$ from the task alone, a *reward-guided revision* using the
RewardPack and terminal Critic review, and a *hypothesis-guided
candidate* whose actor receives guidance from a Hypothesis module but
neither the RewardPack nor the other candidates. The complete
candidate-generation protocol is specified in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Implementation details ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
In this second Jury role, three members rank all candidates generated so
far from their artifacts and receipts, and a reducer adjudicates the
rankings against the evidence, giving an order $`\succ`$. The selector
chooses among the current round’s candidates $`\mathcal{Y}_{n}`$ and
keeps $`y^{\circ}`$ unless one ranks strictly above it without a known
regression:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y^{\star}=\max\nolimits_{\succ}\bigl(\{y^{\circ}\}\cup\mathcal{Y}^{+}\bigr),\qquad\mathcal{Y}^{+}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}:\ y\succ y^{\circ},\ \text{no test of $R$ that $y^{\circ}$ passes fails on $y$}\}.
``` |  | (6) |

We call $`y^{\star}`$ *Selected by reward*; ties are broken as in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Implementation details ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
The selector sees no benchmark scores or grading receipts. The reward
enters selection as evidence for the Jury and as a test-level veto, not
as a scalar score; the order agreement in
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
evaluates the reward’s own pass-share ordering
([Section 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")),
not the Jury’s ranking. Each round therefore makes many more model calls
than a single actor run, across the Jury, Builder, QC, Critic, and
ranking roles;
[Section D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Compute resources and costs ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
explains why we report no total-cost or equal-budget comparison.

## 4 Experiments

We ask three questions in
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"):
does Reward Engine improve the delivered artifact; does the frozen
reward select better candidates than reward-free policies; and does its
ordering agree with the benchmark grader’s?
[Section E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Sensitivity analyses ‣ Appendix E Additional experimental results ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
reports sensitivity analyses.

### 4.1 Experimental setup

##### Benchmarks.

*WorkBuddy Bench Office* has 50 mixed-format office tasks scored 0–100
by deterministic rules and a model judge \[[Tencent Youtu Lab et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17)\]. *Claw-Eval* provides executable environments and
human-checked rubrics \[[Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Claw-Eval
Contributors, 2026](#bib.bib16)\]; we use 104 frozen task versions from
68 scenarios (36 bilingual pairs), scored 0–100 by its native grader
with a custom judge
([Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

##### Compared outputs.

Each task is executed in sequential rounds. In every round, the system
generates a fresh task-only candidate from the public task alone, a
reward-guided revision that also receives the RewardPack and terminal
Critic review, and a hypothesis-guided candidate; the selector then
returns Selected by reward
([Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
We compare Selected by reward with Baseline, Revision, uniform choice
among the generated candidates, and an Oracle that selects the candidate
with the highest benchmark score. Baseline and policy aggregation are
defined in
[Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Baseline and compared policies ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"),
and the complete candidate-generation protocol is given in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Implementation details ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").

##### Metrics.

We report mean score, average pass rate, three-run success coverage
($`\mathrm{pass@3}`$), and three-run consistency
($`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$), together with paired 95% confidence intervals
that resample WorkBuddy Bench Office tasks or Claw-Eval scenarios. For
selection, we additionally report regret to the oracle and the share of
the uniform-to-oracle gap recovered. Metric definitions, aggregation,
and statistical procedures are specified in
[Sections D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Baseline and compared policies ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
and [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents");
per-round performance is reported in
[Section E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Per-round results ‣ Appendix E Additional experimental results ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").

##### Selected by reward has the highest mean score and coverage on both benchmarks.

It has the highest mean score on WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval
([Table 1](#S4.T1 "In 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")),
gaining $`+2.03`$ ($`[0.90,3.21]`$) on Claw-Eval and $`+1.16`$
($`[-1.60,3.96]`$) on WorkBuddy Bench Office, where the interval
includes zero. It also has the highest success coverage, reaching every
Claw-Eval task at least once ($`\mathrm{pass@3}=100\%`$), and raises
$`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$ from 45.00% to 54.00% and from 78.37% to 83.65%
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents");
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")a,b).

##### Failures fall most on Claw-Eval.

Relative to Baseline, the run failure rate falls by 37.5% on Claw-Eval,
with an interval excluding zero, and by 14.0% on WorkBuddy Bench Office,
with an interval including zero
([Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")c).
The per-task distributions retain both gains and losses
([Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")d,e).
Always delivering the revision attains the highest $`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$
(56.00% and 87.50%) but a lower mean and coverage, so selection trades
some consistency for higher average quality.

##### Does the frozen reward select better candidates?

All policies choose among the same generated candidates, so selection
quality can be compared on equal footing. Selecting by the frozen reward
gains $`+1.83`$ ($`[0.22,3.61]`$) over uniform choice on WorkBuddy Bench
Office and $`+2.36`$ ($`[1.56,3.20]`$) on Claw-Eval, recovering 25.76%
and 39.40% of the uniform-to-oracle gap
([Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Failures fall most on Claw-Eval. ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
Its mean regret, 5.29 and 3.63, is the lowest among the non-oracle
policies, compared with 6.40 and 4.13 for always revising.

##### Does the reward agree with the benchmark grader?

We re-evaluate candidates against frozen RewardPacks and compare their
within-task orderings with the benchmark grader. Order agreement, the
share of grader-ordered candidate pairs that the reward does not
reverse, is 82.33% on WorkBuddy Bench Office and 80.53% on Claw-Eval,
and 84.69% and 81.72% on distinguishable tasks
([Table 4](#S4.T4 "In Does the frozen reward select better candidates? ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
The packs may have seen evaluated candidates; this analysis does not
measure generalization to unseen candidates.

## 5 Related work

##### Judges, rubrics, and verifiers.

Model judges scale open-ended evaluation but are sensitive to position
and presentation \[[Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib33)\]. Fine-grained rubric judges \[[Kim et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34)\], rubrics and checklists as rewards \[[Gunjal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10); [Viswanathan et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)\], reusable
rubric evaluation \[[Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026](#bib.bib11)\], and
natural-language unit tests \[[Saad-Falcon et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)\]
make criteria explicit, and Agent-as-a-Judge adds agentic inspection
\[[Zhuge et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)\]. Trained verifiers and process
reward models score solutions or steps \[[Cobbe et al.,
2021](#bib.bib23); [Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25)\], and AgentRewardBench documents disagreement between
automatic and expert judgments of web-agent trajectories \[[Lù et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)\]. Our unit of evaluation is instead a criterion bound
to an executed procedure whose receipt names the artifact, scope, and
version, with explicit status for errors and unresolved evidence.

##### Constructing and repairing rewards.

Language models can design rewards from descriptions \[[Kwon et al.,
2023](#bib.bib29)\] and write reward code refined with training feedback
\[[Ma et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Xie et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)\]; CodeT
selects programs with generated tests \[[Chen et al.,
2023](#bib.bib31)\]; and EvoRubrics co-evolves rubrics adversarially
with the policy \[[Ding et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)\]. Reward Engine
instead tests the reward against counterexamples before use, gates
repairs by regression on accumulated cases as in software regression
testing, and freezes the result while it is used
([Table 5](#A1.T5 "In Appendix A Comparison with related methods ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
Freezing fixes the standard but does not remove proxy misspecification,
since a fixed proxy can still be overoptimized or hacked \[[Skalse et
al., 2022](#bib.bib27); [Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib26); [Pan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)\].

##### Feedback, refinement, and persistent experience.

Self-Refine, Reflexion, CRITIC, and TextGrad revise outputs or system
components with language feedback \[[Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib2);
[Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib1); [Gou et al., 2024](#bib.bib18);
[Yuksekgonul et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)\], although re-prompting alone can
account for gains attributed to critique \[[Stechly et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)\]. ExpeL, ADAS, and SkillRL retain lessons, agent
designs, or skills \[[Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib9); [Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)\], and Constitutional
AI, PPO, and GRPO update parameters from feedback or rewards \[[Bai et
al., 2022](#bib.bib6); [Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib12); [Shao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib13)\]. Reward Engine exposes the measurement behind
its feedback, and its persistent target is evaluator construction rather
than task solving.

## 6 Conclusion

Reward Engine makes reward construction part of solving open-ended tool
tasks. From public task requirements and execution experience, it builds
evidence-grounded checks for required correctness and graded quality,
tests them against counterexamples, and holds the resulting reward fixed
while it guides revision and selection. Updates between rounds
incorporate new evidence without changing the standard during use. On
WorkBuddy Bench Office and Claw-Eval, this approach raises three-run
consistency over Baseline and improves selection over uniform choice
among the same candidates by 1.83 and 2.36 points, respectively, with
95% confidence intervals excluding zero. Mean delivery gains over
Baseline are clearest on Claw-Eval. The constructed reward also does not
reverse the benchmark graders’ ordering on over 80% of evaluated
candidate pairs. These results support constructing and validating
rewards as a practical route to improving tool-agent outputs at
inference time. Applying the same reward interface to reinforcement
learning is a direction for future work.

## Appendix contents

[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Comparison with related methods ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
compares Reward Engine with related methods,
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
gives the notation, RewardPack schema, and implementation details, and
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
proves the regression-gate invariant.
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
describes the benchmarks, baselines, implementation, statistical
procedures, grading provenance, and recorded costs.
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Additional experimental results ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
supports each main-text result in the order of
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"):
delivery quality, per-round results, sensitivity analyses, selection,
agreement with the benchmark grader, and auxiliary measurement case
studies.

In method-comparison tables, bold marks the best displayed point
estimate among comparable methods, including ties. Higher scores and
success rates, and lower regret and error rates, are preferred. Oracle
upper bounds and label-defining comparators are excluded; bold does not
imply statistical significance.

## Appendix A Comparison with related methods

[Table 5](#A1.T5 "In Appendix A Comparison with related methods ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
compares Reward Engine with the evaluators and reward-construction
methods discussed in
[Section 5](#S5 "5 Related work ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
on the properties that define its reward. Marks describe each method as
specified and evaluated in the cited work, not extensions it could
support; feedback and experience methods, which revise the actor rather
than the evaluator, are discussed only in
[Section 5](#S5 "5 Related work ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
Most methods already keep the evaluator fixed while it is used. What
distinguishes Reward Engine is the combination of evidence receipts,
per-task counterexample testing, and a regression gate. These make
evaluator failures visible and keep repairs from losing earlier
agreement, but they do not by themselves make the reward correct: the
gate holds only on generated cases with fallible reference labels
([Proposition 1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Ratchet). ‣ C.1 Ratchet property ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Method |  Executable checks^(a) |  Evidence receipts^(b) |  Counterexample testing^(c) |  Regression gate^(d) |  Frozen during use^(e) |  Reported use |
| Judges, rubrics, and verifiers |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  LLM-as-a-judge \[[Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)\] |  No |  No |  No |  No |  — |  Evaluation |
|  Prometheus \[[Kim et al., 2024](#bib.bib34)\] |  No |  No |  No |  No |  — |  Evaluation |

|  Agent-as-a-Judge \[[Zhuge et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)\] |  No |  Part. |  No |  No |  — |  Evaluation |

|  Trained verifiers \[[Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib23), [Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib24), [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)\] |  No |  No |  No |  No |  Yes |  Reranking |
| Constructing and repairing rewards |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  LM reward design \[[Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib29)\] |  No |  No |  No |  No |  Yes |  RL |

^(a)Each criterion is bound to a stored, re-runnable procedure (code or
a tool recipe). Reward Engine’s procedures include model judgments over
located evidence, so executability does not imply a deterministic
oracle. Checklist feedback writes verifier programs only for items it
can check exactly and averages them with judge scores.

^(b)Each judgment retains the inspected evidence and separates
unresolved or failed measurement from a violation. Autorubric records a
per-criterion explanation and an explicit cannot-assess verdict;
Agent-as-a-Judge gathers workspace evidence for each requirement.

^(c)The evaluator for a task is tested on labeled counterexamples before
use. Several works measure agreement with human labels in aggregate
\[[Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib7), [Zhuge et al., 2025](#bib.bib8), [Rao
and Callison-Burch, 2026](#bib.bib11), [Lù et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)\];
EvoRubrics adapts its rubric generator adversarially during training
rather than testing it on labeled cases.

^(d)A revision is accepted only if no previously agreed case is lost;
for Reward Engine this holds on generated cases with fallible reference
labels
([Proposition 1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Ratchet). ‣ C.1 Ratchet property ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

^(e)The evaluator is fixed while a policy is trained, reranked, or
revised against it, that is, during optimization. Eureka and Text2Reward
fix the reward within each training run and revise it between runs, as
Reward Engine does between rounds; EvoRubrics updates its rubrics at
every training step.

Table 5: Properties of evaluators and reward-construction methods as
evaluated in the cited work. Yes: provided; Part.: partially provided
(see notes); No: not provided; —: not applicable, because the work only
evaluates and nothing is optimized against the evaluator.

This section gives the notation, the RewardPack schema, and the
implementation details behind the construction, repair, and use stages
summarized in
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
[Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
shows the evaluated configuration; Builder appears there as Reward
Builder and Harness Builder, and QC as Adversarial Testing and Repair &

### B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics

A RewardPack stores one reward version
$`R_{v}=\{(c_{i},\kappa_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}`$ together with its scope,
version metadata, and repair ledger;
[Table 7](#A2.T7 "In B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
lists the stored records.

|  Record |  Producer |  Fields |
|----|----|----|
|  Criterion ($`c_{i}`$) |  Jury |  Identifier; standard; hard or soft kind with its origin and evidence; applicability and priority rationale; measurement question; subrequirements; fail, partial, and full anchors. |
|  Test binding ($`\kappa_{i}`$) |  Builder |  Test and criterion identifiers; checker key, which a registry dispatches to a function or model evaluator; arguments; question; rubric; optional tool recipe of tool calls and restricted computations. |
|  Measurement record (receipt $`e_{i}`$) |  Harness |  Artifact and environment snapshots; scope; reward and check versions; input references; procedure type; observations; judgment; execution status. |
|  Scope |  Caller |  Applicable requirements and conversation, admitted sources, user amendments, and environment assumptions. |
|  Version metadata |  QC |  Version identity and hash; parent version; changed criteria and checks; fresh measurements; review records bound to the identity, scope, and hash; selection rationale. |
|  Repair ledger ($`Q_{v}`$) |  QC |  Case identity; material (artifact and history); case type (control, error, or boundary); targeted criterion; reference label; agreement recorded once per version and replayed. |

Table 7: Records stored in a RewardPack. Every published criterion has
at least one bound test; obligations that are deferred or cannot be
mapped remain unknown in a separate coverage ledger.

##### Judgment semantics.

For criterion $`i`$ with bound tests $`\ell\in L_{i}`$, the judgment is
the tuple $`z_{i}=(z_{i\ell})_{\ell\in L_{i}}`$ with
$`z_{i\ell}\in\mathcal{Z}_{i\ell}\cup\{\bot\}`$ binary or graded; the
single-test judgments of
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
are the case $`|L_{i}|=1`$. Three outcomes are kept apart throughout: a
failing judgment records an observed violation, $`\bot`$ records
insufficient evidence, and a parser or tool exception is an execution
error, recorded in the receipt $`e_{i}`$, that establishes neither a
violation nor its cause. No scalar is imposed. A consumer that needs one
supplies a reduction rule, under which $`(\mathsf{pass},\bot)`$ earns no
implicit partial credit and an all-unknown tuple remains unresolved;
hard or soft kinds and priorities imply no global weights, vetoes, or
aggregation rule. A receipt may be reused only if its artifact,
environment snapshot, requirement scope, and check version all match the
current measurement. This is admissibility for reuse, not semantic
truth, and it cannot supply missing observations, so a modified workbook
needs fresh receipts and a checker repair keeps only receipts whose
bindings still match.

##### Information boundary.

Construction and feedback use only $`\mathcal{I}`$
([Section 2](#S2 "2 Problem setup ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).
Genuine user updates enter $`\mathcal{I}`$, and internal suggestions
never add requirements. Hidden answers and grader outputs are excluded
by design. Public benchmark materials that an actor retrieves count as
public knowledge
([Table 12](#A5.T12 "In E.3.1 WorkBuddy Bench Office score sensitivity ‣ E.3 Sensitivity analyses ‣ Appendix E Additional experimental results ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")).

### B.3 Construction and regression-gated repair

##### Jury.

Three Jury members draft obligations from the public requirements and
permitted knowledge, then reconsider them against the initial task-only
artifacts. Each phase needs at least two usable drafts; missing outputs
do not count as agreement, and too few drafts or a failed reduction
yield no publishable specification. A reducer merges both phases, and
validation maps, defers, or excludes with a reason every identified
obligation. Obligations that were never proposed remain a semantic
omission risk that validation cannot detect. Knowledge, strategies, and
QC hypotheses may suggest checks but do not establish requirements.

##### Builder and delivery contracts.

Builder produces the bindings in
[Table 7](#A2.T7 "In B.2 RewardPack schema and judgment semantics ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
under the caller’s scope, construction budget, and delivery contract,
returning an admissible RewardPack or an explicit construction failure
that remains in the delivery denominator. The Outcome contract requires
schema, binding, and smoke checks and permits synthetic fixtures.
Publication additionally requires a receipt for every bound test on a
real artifact, not all of them errors, a completed review, and a
selection rationale. The artifact must come from a sandboxed actor run
charged to construction or a verified archive captured before grading.

##### Self-attack and repair.

Adversarial review executes the control, error, and boundary cases of
[Section 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
Reference models label anonymized material against public task evidence,
blind to the RewardPack, the attack rationale, and the predicted labels,
and replay preserves case identities and material. Beyond
[Eq. 4](#S3.E4 "In 3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"),
the implementation accepts a candidate only if known reference labels
are unchanged and fresh boundary cases around the repair are supported;
otherwise the incumbent is kept. Structural review checks bindings but
not semantics, so a rebuild without adversarial review leaves its
semantic correction unverified. QC routes confirmed checker defects to
Builder, missing or mis-stated obligations to Jury, and independently
established artifact defects to actor feedback, and leaves uncertain
attributions unresolved; infrastructure failures permit bounded
remeasurement. A checker repair preserves the criteria and unrelated
checks, and a criterion repair remeasures only the affected bindings.
Defects found while a reward is in use are queued and never modify the
active version. The BoundaryUpdate operation in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Candidates and selection. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
keeps, rebuilds, or revises the reward at a round boundary under
comparison and tie rules fixed by the caller, carrying forward the
repair ledger. It records the resulting reward as the next version
$`R_{v+1}`$; retaining the incumbent leaves the reward contents
unchanged. These boundary transitions follow the caller’s rules rather
than
[Eq. 4](#S3.E4 "In 3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
After QC, the latest version is frozen for the execution segment.

### B.4 Execution with a frozen reward

##### Segments and Critic.

An execution segment starts from a caller-supplied context $`h_{0}`$ and
ends at completion, budget exhaustion, or a scope change; output edits
within a segment are remeasured under the frozen reward, whereas a
change of requirements, admitted sources, or environment assumptions
starts a new segment. Critic abstains, suggests, or requests
clarification, citing evidence for each claimed gap and preserving
criterion and test identifiers, evidence references, and error status;
missing evidence prompts verification rather than a verdict.
TerminalReviewLoop in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Candidates and selection. ‣ 3.3 Using a frozen reward ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
applies terminal review, feedback-driven continuation, and rechecking to
the reward-guided candidate under the frozen reward; ordinary actor
steps append only actions and observations. The operation returns the
final actor context, including its delivery and any unresolved status.
The evaluated revision budget, stopping conditions, and selection rule
are specified in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Implementation details ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").

##### Memory retrieval.

Memory retrieves up to three entries into the construction context by
sparse cosine similarity over task, requirements, checks, and gaps; each
entry records its sources, applicability, validation status, and
limitations.

### B.5 Prompt templates

The boxes give abridged semantic prompts for the construction,
measurement, terminal-feedback, and ranking calls. Task-specific content
is represented by named inputs; these are not verbatim transcripts of
every historical run. Exact payloads remain in archived request records.
Shared evidence rules apply to every role, while the evaluated call
schedule and revision limits are specified in
[Section D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Implementation details ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").

## Appendix C Theoretical Analysis

### C.1 Ratchet property

###### Proposition 1 (Ratchet).

If $`R_{v+1}`$ is obtained from $`R_{v}`$ by the acceptance rule
[Eq. 4](#S3.E4 "In 3.2 Self-attack and regression-gated repair ‣ 3 Reward Engine ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"),
then $`G_{v}\subseteq G_{v+1}`$, and $`|G_{v+1}|\geq|G_{v}|+1`$ when the
candidate is accepted. Hence, along such transitions, a case on which
the reward once agreed with its reference label is never lost, and at
most $`|Q|-|G_{0}|`$ repairs are accepted, where $`Q`$ is the final
ledger.

###### Proof of [Proposition 1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Ratchet). ‣ C.1 Ratchet property ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Analysis ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").

Judgments are recorded once per version and replayed, so $`G_{v}`$ is
fixed given $`v`$, and on $`Q_{v}`$ the recorded judgments of
$`R_{v+1}`$ are those of $`\widetilde{R}`$ if it is accepted and those
of $`R_{v}`$ otherwise. Since $`Q_{v}\subseteq Q_{v+1}`$, this gives
$`G_{v+1}\supseteq\widetilde{G}`$ after acceptance and
$`G_{v+1}\supseteq G_{v}`$ after rejection. After acceptance, the
no-regression clause gives $`\widetilde{G}\supseteq G_{v}`$, so
$`G_{v}\subseteq G_{v+1}`$ in both cases. The fixes-a-failure clause
further supplies some $`j^{\ast}\in F_{v}\cap\widetilde{G}`$; as
$`R_{v}`$ disagrees on $`j^{\ast}`$, we have
$`j^{\ast}\in G_{v+1}\setminus G_{v}`$, so $`|G_{v+1}|\geq|G_{v}|+1`$.
Each accepted repair thus adds at least one case to a set contained in
$`Q`$, so at most $`|Q|-|G_{0}|`$ repairs are accepted. ∎

The statement concerns the set $`G_{v}`$; the agreement *rate* on
$`Q_{v}`$ can still fall when an attack round adds failing cases. It is
a property of the acceptance rule, not of the attacker: it says nothing
about cases that were never generated, and a systematically wrong
reference label is ratcheted in as easily as a correct one.
Round-boundary updates follow the caller’s rules
([Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Construction and regression-gated repair ‣ Appendix B Method details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"))
and are covered only when they pass the same gate. Held-out evaluation
of the frozen reward against independent labels addresses these gaps.

## Appendix D Experimental details

### D.1 Benchmarks

#### D.1.1 WorkBuddy Bench Office

WorkBuddy Bench Office is the Office subset of a role-based benchmark
whose other subsets cover Code, Web, and Security \[[Tencent Youtu Lab
et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)\]. We use all 50 tasks of the version-1.0
Office subset with equal weight. They involve spreadsheets, CSV, PDF,
and word-processing documents (24 data/file operations, 17 document
operations, and nine workspace-automation tasks), and their difficulty
lies in data relationships, document structure, state, and supporting
evidence rather than file size. Agents run in a sandboxed Docker
workspace through Harbor. The CompositeVerifier combines deterministic
checks on the submitted artifacts with a model judge over extracted
evidence through a task-specific weighted sum; across our 150 final
receipts, the deterministic weight ranges from 0.70 to 0.95. A run
passes at 80 (inclusive). These external graders are distinct from the
internal RewardPack measurements. Among 450 round-candidate records, the
only invalid score is the initial-round task-only score on
analyst-forecast-extract-L3-018, archived as 72.8 with an
invalid-scoring flag; we count it as zero and retain the raw value and
flag. Selection returned the revision in that round, so it is
unaffected.

#### D.1.2 Claw-Eval

Claw-Eval evaluates autonomous agents on tasks with executable
environments and human-checked rubrics \[[Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib15),
[Claw-Eval Contributors, 2026](#bib.bib16)\]. It contains 300 tasks and
2,159 rubrics across nine categories (161 general, 101 multimodal, and
38 multi-turn tasks), provides sandboxed services, records trajectories,
and distinguishes completion, safety, and robustness; its leaderboard
uses $`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$ over three independent trials. We use 104
frozen task versions from 68 scenarios, including 36 bilingual pairs,
scored on the continuous 0–100 native scale with a custom model judge; a
run passes at 75 (inclusive). Each task version is evaluated over three
sequential rounds of task-only, revision, and hypothesis-guided
candidates, yielding 936 graded round candidates. Baseline repetition
and aggregation are defined in
[Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Baseline and compared policies ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
Our empirical three-run success metrics follow the aggregation in
[Sections D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Baseline and compared policies ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
and [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents");
the sequential rounds are dependent, unlike the leaderboard’s
independent-trial protocol.

### D.2 Baseline and compared policies

Baseline uses two repetitions of three task-only runs per task (six
executions). In every run, the same actor receives only the public task
and its attachments. For a three-run statistic $`g`$
([Section D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents"))
and native score $`s^{(q)}_{ir}`$ of task $`i`$ in repetition $`q`$ and
run $`r`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{i}(\mathrm{Baseline})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=1}^{2}g\bigl(s^{(q)}_{i1},s^{(q)}_{i2},s^{(q)}_{i3}\bigr).
``` |  |

Revision, hypothesis guidance, and Selected by reward apply $`g`$ to
their three sequential rounds. We write $`s_{i}(A)`$ for the task-level
mean score of method $`A`$; aggregation precedes paired resampling.
Uniform choice averages the three candidates per task-round; Oracle
takes their maximum benchmark score. Headroom is
$`(\text{policy}-\text{uniform})/(\text{oracle}-\text{uniform})`$.

### D.3 Implementation details

|  Benchmark |  Candidate generation and models |  External grading |
|----|----|----|
|  WorkBuddy Bench Office |  Three sequential iterations, each producing task-only, reward-guided revision, and hypothesis-guided candidates; results are aggregated across all three iterations. Actor: DeepSeek V4 Flash. |  Official task-specific composite of deterministic rules and a model judge (rule weight 0.70–0.95). |
|  Claw-Eval |  Three sequential rounds of fresh candidates with same-task pool, checks, memory, and RewardPack carryover. Actor: DeepSeek V4 Flash; Jury and proposal roles also use MiniMax, Qwen, and GLM models. |  Native grader with a custom DeepSeek V4 Flash judge. |

Table 8: Evaluated configuration. On both benchmarks, the reward-guided
revision permits at most two revisions with at most three targeted
checks per review, and the task-only and hypothesis-guided candidates
have delivery review disabled. Baseline repetition and aggregation are
defined in
[Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Baseline and compared policies ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").

##### Candidates.

Each round launches a fresh task-only actor that receives only the
public task and its attachments. The reward-guided revision additionally
receives the current RewardPack and terminal Critic review: a model
overview proposes up to three targeted checks per review, and each
nonempty review permits one continuation in the same actor session
followed by a recheck, with at most two revisions. Measurement, Critic
calls, and continuations consume the execution budget. Revision stops
early only when the current overview reports no gaps, nothing is
deferred or carried over, and the selected checks and all blocking
requirements pass; unselected checks remain unverified, so stopping does
not certify full-pack coverage. When the budget is exhausted, the latest
artifact is kept with its unresolved status. The hypothesis-guided
candidate receives guidance from a Hypothesis module but neither the
RewardPack nor the candidate pool. Before each round, the module reads
the public task, Jury gaps, permitted knowledge, and same-task artifacts
and checks from earlier rounds, and returns fallible guidance (a method,
an optional target, the expected benefit, a verification plan, and
clarification questions) or a keep decision, which reduces the candidate
to task-only generation. On WorkBuddy Bench Office the archive records
the guidance as applied on 41 tasks, a keep decision on two, and an
unknown state on seven. Because the surrounding loop accumulates
candidates, measurements, memory, and Jury decisions, “task-only”
describes the actor’s prompt, not independence from the loop.

##### Selection.

Three Jury members compare the candidates. A valid record places every
candidate exactly once, in an ordered tie group or an unknown list, with
artifact references and reasons; abstention is valid, whereas malformed
output is not. A model reducer adjudicates at least two valid records
against the evidence without counting votes, using ties for unsupported
differences and unknowns for insufficient evidence. The terminal Jury
ranks all accumulated candidates, but the selector chooses among the
current round’s three: the highest-ranked candidate strictly ahead of
the task-only candidate with no known failure on a test, matched by
identifier, that the task-only candidate passes, with eligible ties
favoring the revision over the hypothesis-guided candidate; otherwise
the task-only candidate.

### D.4 Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis

Success thresholds are $`\eta=80`$ for WorkBuddy Bench Office and
$`\eta=75`$ for Claw-Eval.

For a three-run group with benchmark scores $`s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}`$ and
successes $`b_{r}=\mathbf{1}[s_{r}\geq\eta]`$, the three-run statistics
$`g`$ are the mean score, average pass rate, success coverage, and
consistency:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1}{3}\sum_{r=1}^{3}s_{r},\qquad\frac{1}{3}\sum_{r=1}^{3}b_{r},\qquad b_{1}\vee b_{2}\vee b_{3},\qquad b_{1}\wedge b_{2}\wedge b_{3}.
``` |  |

Method-specific task-level aggregation is defined in
[Section D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Baseline and compared policies ‣ Appendix D Experimental details ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents").
After that aggregation, task averages of coverage and consistency give
$`\mathrm{pass@3}`$ and $`\mathrm{Pass}^{3}`$, respectively. Over the
task set $`\mathcal{T}`$, we report task-averaged scores
$`\bar{s}(A)=|\mathcal{T}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}s_{i}(A)`$ and
paired differences from Baseline,
$`\Delta(A)=|\mathcal{T}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\bigl(s_{i}(A)-s_{i}(\mathrm{Baseline})\bigr)`$.

Paired 95% percentile intervals use 200,000 resamples of WorkBuddy Bench
Office tasks (NumPy default generator, seed 20260915) or the 68
Claw-Eval scenario clusters (seed 20261005), preserving bilingual task
versions and all observations belonging to each sampled unit; sampled
task versions receive equal weight. Differences of at most $`10^{-8}`$
count as ties for W/T/L, the two-sided sign test (which excludes ties),
and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Scores are never rounded before
comparison. Intervals are nominal and unadjusted for multiple
comparisons. Claw-Eval task-level tests do not account for bilingual
dependence; its uncertainty is assessed with the scenario-cluster
intervals.

Relative failure reduction is
$`100\bigl(1-\frac{1-\bar{p}(A)}{1-\bar{p}(\mathrm{Baseline})}\bigr)`$,
where $`\bar{p}(A)`$ is the task-averaged pass rate of method $`A`$ at
the reporting threshold. Both pass rates are recomputed together in each
of the same 200,000 paired bootstrap draws; no draw has zero Baseline
failure rate. This statistic and the absolute pass-rate difference
summarize the same outcomes. The per-task gains in
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")d,e
are $`s_{i}(\text{Selected by reward})-s_{i}(\mathrm{Baseline})`$;
values within $`10^{-8}`$ of zero are ties.

### D.5 Grading provenance and reproducibility

##### WorkBuddy Bench Office score provenance.

Archived deliveries requiring native scores were restored from their
exact workspaces. We matched candidate identities and artifact records
and verified inventory SHA-256 hashes, including six reused deliveries.
On October 6, 2026, we ran the original task-specific rule checks in
isolated task Docker environments and the native rubric judge with
DeepSeek V4 Flash via OpenLux. No actor was rerun and no delivered
artifact was revised. Native technical retries and format repair were
retained; scores were not retried for quality. Source bindings, grader
receipts, errors, and request/response bodies (except the first smoke
run, which retains verdicts) are archived separately. This later grading
introduces temporal judge and environment variation; bootstrap intervals
condition on accepted scores and do not capture fresh-judge variability.

### D.6 Compute resources and costs

The available token records cover auxiliary offline analyses, including
failed attempts, rather than the complete benchmark workflow. Actor
execution, reward construction, candidate generation, selection, and
grading are not covered by a complete, non-overlapping cost ledger, and
timing records omit some calls and retries. These records therefore
support no total-cost, throughput, or equal-budget comparison.

### E.4 Selection analysis

[Table 13](#A5.T13 "In E.4 Selection analysis ‣ Appendix E Additional experimental results ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
gives the full policy comparison on the generated candidate pools;
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Failures fall most on Claw-Eval. ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Reward Engine: Reward-CentricSelf-Evolution for Open-Ended Tool Agents")
summarizes gains over uniform choice. Relative to always returning the
revision, selection gains $`+1.11`$ ($`[-0.34,2.75]`$) on WorkBuddy
Bench Office and $`+0.50`$ ($`[-1.01,2.21]`$) on Claw-Eval, so neither
interval establishes superiority over that fixed policy. Selection finds
a best candidate in 74/150 and 183/312 task-rounds, versus 73/150 and
206/312 for revision. Thus, on Claw-Eval it hits a best candidate less
often but has lower average regret; revision recovers 10.13% and 31.03%
of the uniform-to-oracle gap on the two benchmarks. These comparisons
characterize the selector as a whole and exclude candidate-generation
costs: the archive does not identify how often rankings relied on
receipts rather than artifact text. A compute-matched comparison with
repeated sampling and a generic model selector remains untested.
````
